strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: controllable, compositional generation of 3D anatomical segmentations for biophysical simulation, without requiring retraining for new constraint combinations.

The core idea of guiding an unconditional diffusion model with differentiable, geometrically-normalized moment losses (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) applied per-component is simple, clean, and well-motivated, and enables disentangled control (Algorithm 1, Sec 4).

Extensive experimental evaluation, including conditional fidelity, morphological distribution similarity (pair plots, Frechet distance), point-cloud metrics (MMD/COV/1-NNA), a disentanglement ablation (Table 1), and a compositional-generation comparison against a strong dropout-based conditional baseline (Table 2), which the proposed method generally outperforms, especially with few constrained components.

Reasonably comprehensive set of baselines for comparison (explicit/implicit conditioning with ANG, cross-attention with CFG), which strengthens the claim that inference-time guidance outperforms training-time conditioning for flexible constraint composition.

A compelling downstream demonstration linking geometric guidance to biomechanical simulation (RV inpainting and FEM pressurization), illustrating practical utility for form-function studies, plus reasonably thorough appendix with implementation details supporting reproducibility.
Clear writing and figures that effectively illustrate the qualitative behavior of the method (disentangled control, compositionality).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single anatomical domain (cardiac CT segmentations from TotalSegmentator, one dataset, one VAE/LDM backbone), raising questions about generality to other anatomies or modalities; no experiments on a second dataset/organ system to support claims of broad applicability.

The geometric guidance is limited to fairly coarse, low-order moments (mass/volume, centroid, second-order covariance ellipsoid); complex or non-ellipsoidal shape variation (e.g., branching vasculature, local curvature) is only qualitatively shown (Fig. 12) without quantitative assessment of fidelity for such structures.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline are sometimes marginal (e.g., Table 2 at higher component counts, geometric guidance and implicit conditioning are comparable), and the paper's own text acknowledges this ("performance of implicit conditioning is similar to that of geometric guidance" at higher component counts), somewhat weakening the generality of the compositionality claim.

Hyperparameters (loss weights λ) are tuned experimentally per loss term (Sec 8.4.1) rather than through a principled or automatic procedure, and the paper notes this as a limitation but does not explore sensitivity or robustness of results to these weights beyond a single configuration.

No comparison against more recent/stronger inference-time guidance baselines beyond self-guidance-style loss guidance (e.g., other attribute/text-based guidance schemes cited in Sec 2), and no user study or clinical validation of anatomical plausibility beyond automated morphological/point-cloud metrics.

The biomechanical simulation demonstration (Sec 5.8) is a single toy case study (one patient, RV enlargement/shrinkage) without quantitative validation against ground truth or broader cohort-level analysis, limiting the strength of claims about enabling counterfactual biophysical studies.

Some potential instability issues (unstable gradients for near-empty segmentations, need for noise regularization in mass denominator) are mentioned as limitations but not deeply analyzed empirically (e.g., failure rate, frequency of topologically incorrect outputs).

strengths: The core idea of using differentiable geometric moments (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) as an inference-time guidance signal for unconditional anatomical diffusion models is clean, well-motivated, and clearly formalized (Algorithm 1, Eq. 2-7).

The paper provides a fairly thorough set of ablations: disentanglement of size/position/shape control (Table 1, Fig 8-9), multi-component compositional control (Table 2, Fig 10-11), and a qualitative biomechanical simulation demonstration (Fig 13) that connects the method to a concrete downstream use case.

Good visualization and reporting practices: morphological pair-plots, pointcloud metrics (MMD/COV/1-NNA), precision/recall/Fréchet distance are used consistently, and implementation details (hyperparameters, normalization constants, guidance weights) are provided extensively in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

The comparison to conditionally-trained alternatives (explicit/implicit concatenation, cross-attention with CFG/ANG) is a reasonable and relevant set of baselines that highlights the practical benefit of not needing retraining for new constraint combinations.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation is confined to a single anatomical domain (cardiac CT segmentations from TotalSegmentator, only 596 manually curated cases, ~119 in validation), which is a fairly small and narrow dataset; claims of a general framework for '3D anatomy' are not substantiated beyond this one organ system, raising concerns about generalizability to other anatomies (vessels, bone, brain, etc.) with more complex/non-convex topology.

The geometric representation is limited to zeroth/first/second-order moments (essentially an ellipsoid approximation), which is intrinsically unable to capture fine-grained, non-convex, or branching anatomical shape (e.g., vasculature); the paper only shows this qualitatively (Fig 12) without quantitative assessment of fidelity for such structures, and topological correctness (disconnected/duplicated structures) is explicitly listed as an unresolved limitation.

Guidance weight factors (λ0, λ1, λ2) and other hyperparameters (softmax temperature, noise added to mass denominator, dropout rates for baselines) are tuned manually/heuristically per loss in isolation (Section 8.4.1), with no principled or automated approach; this undermines the claim of a simple, easily deployable framework and raises reproducibility/robustness concerns when applied to new constraint combinations or datasets.

The baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation, cross-attention) are all self-implemented adaptations rather than established, independently validated prior methods with released benchmarks; there is no comparison with other existing anatomical generative/shape-control approaches cited in the related work (e.g., statistical shape models, SDF-based cardiac models, other diffusion-guidance methods such as universal guidance), making it hard to judge how the proposed method stands relative to the broader literature.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or repeated-run variance is reported for any of the quantitative tables (Table 1, 2) or line plots, despite results being compared across fairly small numeric gaps in some cases (e.g., FD and 1-NNA differences in Table 2 for higher component counts appear marginal).

The biomechanical simulation application (Section 5.8) is a single toy demonstration with no ground-truth validation, sensitivity analysis, or comparison against real patient outcome data; it is illustrative rather than a rigorous validation of clinical/engineering utility, which weakens the paper's motivating claim about enabling meaningful counterfactual biophysical studies.

The paper acknowledges topology and unstable-gradient issues (empty/near-empty segmentations) but only offers ad hoc mitigations (adding noise to the mass denominator) rather than a principled solution, and defers proper topological regularization to future work, leaving an important robustness gap unaddressed.

strengths: Proposes a training-free, inference-time guidance framework for controlling unconditional diffusion models of 3D anatomy using differentiable geometric moment losses (mass/size, centroid/position, and scale-normalized covariance/shape), avoiding the need to retrain conditional models for every new constraint.
Demonstrates clear disentangled control over size, shape, and position both quantitatively (Table 1 ablation, ordering effects of each individual loss) and qualitatively (Figures 7-9).

Shows strong compositional generation capability: guidance can be applied to an arbitrary and varying number of anatomical components without retraining, and clearly outperforms an implicit-conditioning baseline with dropout when few components are constrained (Table 2, Figure 11).

Fairly comprehensive experimental comparison against multiple reasonable baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation/heatmap conditioning, cross-attention) combined with standard guidance mechanisms (CFG, adaptive null guidance), using both conditional-fidelity metrics and generative-quality metrics (Fréchet distance, precision/recall, MMD/COV/1-NNA).

Includes a compelling downstream application to biomechanical simulation (RV pressurization FEM) illustrating practical utility for counterfactual/'digital sibling' anatomy generation, which strengthens the significance of the contribution beyond pure generative modeling metrics.
Reasonably detailed appendix covering dataset curation, hyperparameters, guidance/baseline implementation, and evaluation protocol, aiding reproducibility.
Honest discussion of limitations (need for manual weight tuning, gradient instability for near-empty masks, topological artifacts).
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single anatomical domain and dataset (cardiac structures derived from TotalSegmentator CT, 596 cases after filtering); it is unclear how well the moment-based ellipsoidal guidance generalizes to other organs/modalities or to anatomies with more complex, non-ellipsoidal topology (e.g., highly branching vasculature, thin/curved structures) beyond the limited qualitative examples in Figure 12.

The geometric guidance loss weights (λ0, λ1, λ2) are tuned experimentally per loss type rather than derived principledly or learned; this manual tuning burden is acknowledged as a limitation but not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity across datasets/components is not shown).

No runtime/computation-cost comparison between guidance-based sampling (which requires backpropagating through the VAE decoder and moment computation at every denoising step) and the conditionally trained baselines, which is an important practical consideration for adoption of a training-free method.

"Anatomical realism" is assessed purely via morphometric and point-cloud statistical metrics (FD, precision/recall, MMD/COV/1-NNA) without any clinical/expert qualitative validation or downstream task validation beyond the single illustrative biomechanical case study, so claims of clinical plausibility remain only weakly supported.

Topological correctness (disconnected structures, spurious components) is explicitly acknowledged as unresolved and left to future work, which could limit reliability for the stated simulation use-case.

Second-order moments (covariance) only capture coarse ellipsoidal shape approximations; fine-grained or highly non-convex shape control is not really achievable, limiting the expressiveness of the "shape" guidance term relative to more flexible shape representations.

The comparison baselines are conditionally-trained models that must be retrained for each new constraint set, which is somewhat structurally disadvantaged relative to a training-free guidance method by design; a more apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., against other training-free guidance techniques for anatomical geometry, if any exist, or stronger conditional baselines with more expressive conditioning) would strengthen the significance of the reported gains.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: bridges the gap between rigid conditional training and flexible geometric control for anatomical generation, targeting real biophysical simulation use cases (virtual cohorts, digital twins).

Technically clean formulation: differentiable geometric moment functions (zeroth/first/second-order voxel moments for mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) enable interpretable, energy-based guidance of an unconditional latent diffusion model without retraining.

Broad and thorough experimental protocol: multiple quantitative metrics (conditional fidelity L1, morphological precision/recall/FID-like distances, pointcloud MMD/coverage/1-NNA), ablations for disentanglement (size/position/shape independence), multi-part compositionality, dataset-scaling analysis, alternative second-moment decompositions (extent/stretch/orientation), and autoencoder reconstruction bounds.

Demonstrates generality across four distinct anatomical systems (cardiac, aorta, spine, knee) and shows a concrete downstream application via FEM biventricular pressurization simulation on edited anatomy, illustrating practical utility beyond image synthesis.

Extensive, detailed appendix with hyperparameters, dataset curation, and additional analyses supports reproducibility and transparency about design choices and limitations (e.g., Betti-number topological errors, editing scale-factor breakdown).
weaknesses: Inconsistent baseline reporting: three conditional baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation, cross-attention) are introduced, but the key compositionality comparison (Table 1) only reports 'Implicit' vs 'Ours', leaving open whether the strongest possible baseline was used for that comparison.

No wall-clock/computational cost analysis: the method requires backpropagating a geometric loss through the VAE decoder and diffusion denoiser at every sampling step, which likely incurs substantial overhead relative to conditional (single-pass) baselines, but this tradeoff is never quantified.

Quantitative evaluation is concentrated almost entirely on the cardiac dataset; the aorta, spine, and knee datasets (Section 5.8/Figure 12) are only assessed qualitatively, so claims of 'generality over anatomical systems' are not rigorously substantiated.

Guided samples show increased topological (Betti) errors relative to unconditional/reconstructed baselines in several structures (Table 8), indicating the geometric guidance can occasionally degrade anatomical plausibility, a concern only partially addressed as a stated limitation rather than mitigated.

The ellipsoidal/second-moment representation is inherently coarse (captures only up to second-order shape statistics) and cannot express localized or sub-structure geometric features, limiting applicability to more nuanced anatomical control tasks.

Guidance weights require manual per-loss tuning (Table 4), and while the paper claims good transfer across anatomical systems, this is only lightly validated and could be a barrier to practical deployment on novel structures.

Limited statistical rigor: most figures show line/scatter plots without confidence intervals or significance testing across the ~100-200 sample evaluations, making it hard to assess robustness of reported trends.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: enabling inference-time, retraining-free, compositional geometric control of unconditional diffusion models for multi-label 3D anatomical segmentation, which is valuable for in-silico trials and biomechanical simulation workflows.

The proposed differentiable geometric moment losses (zeroth/first/second-order moments for mass, centroid, and scale-normalized covariance) are a clean, interpretable formalization that connects classical morphometrics with energy-based diffusion guidance.

Broad experimental scope: ablations for disentangled single-attribute control, multi-part compositional control, dataset-scaling analysis, autoencoder reconstruction error bounds, editing-scale-factor stress tests, and extension to multiple anatomical systems (cardiac, aorta, spine, knee).
Reasonably thorough appendix with implementation and dataset curation details (hyperparameters, crop sizes, baseline implementations), aiding reproducibility.
Interesting downstream demonstration connecting geometric edits to a biomechanical FEM simulation (RV pressurization), illustrating a concrete use-case beyond pure generative fidelity.
weaknesses: Quantitative superiority over baselines is inconsistent: in Table 1, the 'Implicit' conditional baseline is competitive with or better than the proposed method on several metrics (e.g., Precision/Recall at 1 and 6 constraints, FD and COV at 6 constraints), undermining the central claim that inference-time geometric guidance clearly outperforms conditional training approaches as the number of constrained substructures grows.

Topological fidelity results (Table 8, Appendix 8.10) show that guided sampling can *increase* Betti error (more anatomically implausible disconnected structures) relative to unconditional sampling for several labels (e.g., PA, IVC), which directly works against the stated goal of producing simulation-ready anatomy and is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation rather than addressed.

Generalization claims to other anatomical systems (aorta, spine, knee) rely solely on qualitative figures (Fig. 12) without any quantitative morphological, pointcloud, or conditional-fidelity metrics, which is a weaker standard of evidence than used for the cardiac case and leaves the claim of broad applicability under-supported.

The method requires substantial per-loss manual tuning of guidance weights (λ values spanning orders of magnitude, e.g., 10^4–10^7), and while the paper claims these transfer across anatomies, this is not rigorously demonstrated; the practical burden of tuning for new structures/datasets is understated.

Baselines (explicit/implicit concatenation, cross-attention) are self-implemented adaptations rather than established, independently validated benchmarks, raising some concern about whether they represent fair/strong comparators; no comparison to actual published conditional anatomical diffusion models (e.g., Kadry et al. 2025, SDF4CHD) is provided despite these being discussed as related work.

The core technical contribution is an incremental combination of existing techniques (energy/DPS-style guidance, moment-based shape descriptors, self-guidance for attribute control), with novelty mainly residing in the specific 3D multi-label anatomical application rather than in fundamentally new guidance or modeling machinery.

Downstream biomechanical validation (Figure 11) is a single illustrative case study on one patient with discrete edits, without quantitative comparison to ground truth or a larger cohort, limiting the strength of the claimed clinical/simulation significance.

Dataset sizes for some evaluations are modest (e.g., 596 cardiac cases with 80/20 split, 200 generated samples per condition), and statistical significance/variance of reported metrics is not discussed.

strengths: Proposes a clear, well-motivated inference-time guidance framework that uses differentiable geometric moments (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) to control unconditional anatomical diffusion models without retraining, addressing a genuine gap between flexible but uncontrollable generative models and rigid parametric/conditional approaches.

Demonstrates disentangled control over size, position, and shape, as well as compositional control over an arbitrary number of substructures, with both qualitative (ellipsoid overlay) and quantitative (morphological, pointcloud) evidence.

Broad generality is shown across four distinct anatomical systems (cardiac, aorta, spine, knee), including non-convex and branching structures, supporting the claim that the method is not narrowly tailored to one organ.

Extensive appendix with many informative ablations: dataset-scaling analysis, autoencoder reconstruction error/topology (Betti number) baseline, editing-scale-factor sweep, alternative second-moment decompositions (extent/stretch/orientation), and a toy procedurally generated ellipsoid dataset to isolate the guidance mechanism from anatomical complexity.

Includes a downstream biomechanical simulation case study (biventricular pressurization with inpainted RV edits) that illustrates practical utility for counterfactual form-function studies, beyond pure generative metrics.
Reasonable reproducibility: hyperparameters for VAE/diffusion training, guidance weights, and baseline implementation details are reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: The three compared conditioning baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation, cross-attention) are the authors' own adaptations of prior conditioning ideas rather than established methods evaluated in their original published settings, raising some concern about fairness/tuning parity in the comparison.

Quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: e.g., in Table 1, at higher numbers of constrained substructures the implicit-conditioning baseline is sometimes comparable to or better than the proposed method (e.g., precision/recall and MMD at 6 constraints), which somewhat weakens the claim that the method 'maintains generation quality' better than alternatives.

The approach requires manual, per-loss-term guidance-weight tuning (λ values), and while the authors claim these transfer across anatomical systems, this is only lightly validated and could be a practical burden for new anatomies/datasets.

Topological correctness (disconnected or duplicated substructures) is an acknowledged but unresolved limitation; the Betti-error analysis shows guidance can even increase topological errors for some structures (e.g., PA, IVC), which is concerning for downstream biophysical simulation reliability.
Substructures are restricted to whole label classes or unions thereof and cannot represent localized/sub-regional geometric features (e.g., cross-sections), limiting fine-grained anatomical control.
No analysis of computational overhead/runtime cost of the guidance procedure relative to baselines, which is relevant for practical adoption in simulation pipelines.

Evaluation is purely statistical/morphometric (no clinical expert review or validation against independent ground-truth anatomical variants), and the biomechanical case study is a single illustrative example rather than a systematic validation.
